title: Political Ideologies
tagline: Liberalism and communism: their meanings and defining features, from individual rights to dialectical materialism and the classless society.

overview.intro: An ideology is a coherent set of ideas that explains the political order and prescribes how it should be organised. This unit examines the two that shaped the twentieth century: liberalism, with its emphasis on the individual, rights, democracy and the limits of state power, and communism, with its analysis of class, its account of historical change through dialectical materialism, and its goal of a classless society. Comparing them shows how differently the same questions — freedom, property, equality and the state — can be answered.

learningOutcomes: Define ideology and explain its role in politics.

blocks.text: An ideology is a systematic set of ideas that interprets the political world and offers a programme for its transformation or preservation. Every ideology answers three questions: what human beings are, how society is organised and how it ought to be organised. It differs from a theory in that it is prescriptive as well as descriptive, and from a mere opinion in that its parts hang together, so that a conclusion about property follows from premises about freedom.

The term has acquired two senses. In its pejorative sense an ideology is a set of beliefs held in the face of the evidence, a distortion in the service of an interest. In its neutral sense it is simply a political doctrine, in which case everyone who argues about politics uses one. The exam answer should acknowledge both senses and then work with the neutral one, because the question of whether a doctrine is ideological in the pejorative sense is a separate question about its truthfulness.

items: Ideologies explain what is, prescribe what ought to be and mobilise support.
They supply the vocabulary — liberty, class, nation, justice — in which political claims are made.
Liberalism and communism are the two great competing responses to industrial society.
Criticism of an ideology must engage its strongest form, not its worst adherents.

blocks.text: Liberalism begins with the individual. Society and the state are constituted by persons and exist for their protection, so political authority requires justification in terms of the rights and interests of individuals rather than the other way round. From that premise follow the classical features: liberty understood as freedom from arbitrary interference, the rule of law applying equally to governors and governed, constitutional and representative government with powers divided and limited, protection of property as both an economic right and a bulwark against the state, and religious and intellectual toleration. Mill added the harm principle, that the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community is to prevent harm to others, and his argument for free speech remains the standard case for it.

Liberalism itself divides. Classical liberalism, associated with laissez-faire economics, held that the state should confine itself to security, justice and a minimal set of functions. Welfare liberalism, which became dominant in the twentieth century, accepted that formal liberty is hollow without material security, and therefore accepted regulation, public services and redistribution as conditions of effective freedom rather than as violations of it. The tradition also has internal tensions — between liberty and equality, between the individual and the community — which are the substance of the criticism examined later.

learn.title: Communism, historical materialism and the classless society

blocks.text: Communism rests on the Marxist claim that the economic structure of society determines its political and intellectual life. Historical materialism holds that history advances through the conflict of classes defined by their relation to the means of production: feudalism produced its gravedigger in the bourgeoisie, and capitalism in turn creates the proletariat, a class that owns nothing but its labour and whose interests require the abolition of exploitation itself. The engine of change is dialectical — a mode of production develops, comes into contradiction with the relations of property that enclose it, and is transformed through that contradiction into a new form.

The communist programme follows from the analysis. Private property in the means of production is to be abolished, though not personal possessions, so that the factories and land are held in common; the state, which in existing society serves the ruling class, will wither away once class antagonisms disappear; and the result is a classless society in which production answers to need and human beings are no longer separated from the products of their labour. In the interim a proletarian dictatorship is expected to hold the revolutionary gains. The 1848 Manifesto supplied the famous formulae — the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles, and the working men have no country — and the states that claimed his mantle organised their economies and their politics accordingly.

learn.title: Liberalism and communism compared, and assessed

blocks.text: On liberty the two differ at the root: liberalism treats liberty as a right of individuals to be shielded from power, while the communist tradition treats liberty as inseparable from material conditions and class position, holding that formal freedom without economic independence is the freedom of the worker to sell his labour. On property they divide outright, since for one it is a right and a check on the state and for the other it is the source of exploitation in the means of production. On equality both claim it, but liberalism seeks equal rights and equality before the law with a tolerable distribution, while communism seeks the abolition of class itself. On the state, liberalism limits it but retains it permanently; communism expects it to wither away after class has been abolished.

The assessment should be even-handed in its criticism. Liberalism’s strengths are its tolerance, its protection of the person against arbitrary power and its compatibility with pluralism; its weaknesses are that formal equality can coexist with great material inequality, that rights may protect property more reliably than people, and that its internationalism has often sat alongside empire. Communism’s strengths are its insistence that freedom requires economic security and its analysis of how class shapes political life; its weaknesses are the theory of immiseration, which was contradicted by rising living standards in industrial countries, and the practical record of one-party states that suppressed the very liberties the tradition claimed to complete. Both emerged from the same problem of industrial society, which explains why they still structure the argument rather than merely its history.

questions.explanation: Welfare liberalism holds that formal liberty is hollow without material security, so regulation and public services condition rather than violate freedom.

questions.answer: The worker’s freedom to sell his labour coexists with economic dependence
questions.explanation: Liberty is treated as inseparable from material conditions, so rights that leave economic control concentrated do not produce effective freedom.

questions.prompt: Mill’s rule that power may be used against a member of a civilised community only to prevent harm to others is the harm __________ .
questions.explanation: It marks the boundary between legitimate authority and the liberty of the individual.

questions.prompt: The abolition of class and the withering away of the state is the goal of a classless __________ .
questions.explanation: In the communist programme common ownership replaces class division, so the state ceases to have a class to suppress and administration takes the place of domination.

questions.prompt: State four defining features of liberalism.
questions.answer: Four features are: the primacy of the individual, since the state is justified by the rights it protects; liberty understood as freedom from arbitrary interference; the rule of law, meaning equal, published and prospective rules applied by independent courts; and constitutional government, with limited representative power and divided institutions. Private property as a right and a check on the state, and religious and intellectual toleration, are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each feature must be defined and given one institutional consequence.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by historical materialism.
questions.answer: Historical materialism is the Marxist account of history according to which the economic structure of society — how production is organised and who owns the means of it — conditions its legal, political and intellectual life. History advances through the conflict of classes defined by their position in that structure: feudalism generated lord and serf, capitalism generates bourgeoisie and proletariat. Each mode of production develops its productive forces until they come into contradiction with the relations of property that enclose them, and the contradiction is resolved by a transformation into a new mode of production. The implication is that ideas, law and the state belong to a superstructure determined at base by the economic relations, which is why political change follows economic change rather than leading it.
questions.explanation: Three elements are required: the base–superstructure relation, class struggle as the engine, and contradiction as the mechanism of transition.

questions.prompt: Compare liberalism and communism on liberty, property and the state.
questions.answer: The two ideologies agree that human beings matter politically and then diverge about the conditions of a good society. On liberty, liberalism defines it negatively as freedom from arbitrary interference and secures it through rights, law and constitutional limits, so the state is the danger to be confined. The communist tradition replies that liberty is a positive capacity which depends on material independence: where ownership of the means of production is concentrated, the worker’s formal freedom to contract is exercised under necessity, and the result is dependence rather than self-direction. On property, liberalism treats private property both as an economic right and as a bulwark that prevents the state from becoming the master of every interest, while communism accepts personal possessions but demands the abolition of private property in the means of production, because that is the relation through which surplus is extracted and class is reproduced. On the state, liberalism limits it permanently and constitutionally, dividing its powers and submitting it to elections and law; communism regards the existing state as serving the ruling class and expects it to wither away once class antagonisms themselves disappear, leaving administration in place of domination. The comparison therefore turns on a prior disagreement about whether the individual or the social relation is the basic unit of politics, and each position’s answer to liberty, property and the state follows consistently from that premise.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all three bases compared on both sides with the underlying premise that explains the divergence.

questions.prompt: Both liberalism and communism claimed to answer the problems of industrial society. Which response proved more adequate? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The case for liberalism rests on its record with pluralism and reform. It supplied legal protection against arbitrary power, extended the franchise, tolerated dissent and accommodated the demands of organised labour through parliamentary politics rather than civil war; where it accepted intervention — the welfare measures of the twentieth century — it demonstrated that property and security could be reconciled without abolishing either. Its continuing difficulty is that formal equality has coexisted with severe material inequality, that constitutional rights have often protected ownership more reliably than subsistence, and that liberal states tolerated empire while preaching liberty. The case for communism rests on its analysis: it identified the insecurity, the subordination of labour and the concentration of ownership that industrial society produced, and the states that organised themselves on its principles eliminated unemployment, expanded literacy and industrialised backward economies within a generation. Against that, the same record contains one-party rule, suppressed dissent, the suppression of the very economic rights the tradition promised to complete, and economies that failed to answer consumer need; and Marx’s prediction that immiseration would revolutionaryise the industrial working class was contradicted in the countries where capitalism was oldest, since wages and living standards rose and reformism displaced revolution. The strongest judgement distinguishes the analysis from the prescription: as an account of what industrial society does to people, communism identified real harms that liberalism was slow to address, but as a programme it proved less adequate, because the removal of property rights removed the restraint on state power as well. Liberalism proved more adequate on the balance of liberty and reform, while remaining inadequate on distribution — which is why the durable answers have combined liberal institutions with economic intervention rather than adopting either ideology whole.
questions.explanation: Full marks need evidence from both traditions, criticism of both, and a reasoned judgement that separates analysis from programme.
